extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism educators, linguists, and reading/comprehension researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and teaching news stories so they are logically organized and comprehensible (rather than merely 'readable' or attention-grabbing). Emphasizes discourse-level structure, connectives, sentence relevance, and pedagogical implications for readers' comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize comprehensibility over 'readability'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'script' for writing news stories ought to be overhauled—that comprehensibility ought to be emphasized more than 'readability' (the ability to attract readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching of news writing should de-emphasize the editor's convenience and so‑called readability techniques for seducing the reader into reading entire stories instead of skimming; instead prioritize writing that is actually understandable and digestible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make logical organization and explicit connectives primary determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical organization and explicit connectives should be the most important determinants of the story's form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and teachers can insist that connectives and demarcated structure be privileged over short-sentence tricks or 'human interest'; explicit structure makes stories more skimmable and comprehensible (a linguistics article with connectives can be skimmed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize sentence clarity and relevance over shortness
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to writing good sentences within a story should not be 'Are they short enough?' but 'Is it going to be clear to the reader what the relevance of this information is, what the point of including it is?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sentences by whether they make the relevance of information clear to readers; short sentences that omit connective words can create disconnected lists of facts and impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using quotes and colorful details merely to 'brighten up' a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotes and colorful details used merely to 'brighten up' a story are more likely to attract attention to themselves and away from the news point of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When included for decoration, such elements tend to reduce the story to a jumbled collection of facts. Prefer including quotations/details only when they serve or clarify the story's logical structure or point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let an extreme reading of 'objectivity' ban useful connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are cautioned to attribute to a source every statement not common knowledge, which can lead some reporters to strictly limit logical connectives to those provided by quotable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strict reading of objectivity is inconsistent with the fact that texts directed reporters to learn connectives (accordingly, finally, thus, so, as a consequence). Reporters should use appropriate logical connectives to clarify relations without improperly inserting unattributed interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include causal and logical connectives rather than relying on adjacency
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of causal connectives places the burden of connection entirely on the reader's inference from adjacency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit causal connectives (because, therefore, accordingly, as a consequence) rather than only 'and' or temporal connectives (when, after) that merely imply causal relations; examples show omission makes texts harder to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for producer intentions and pragmatics when analyzing text structure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is futile for text-linguists to look for 'text structure' without taking into account the producer of the text, in particular, the producer's presumable intentions in producing the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourse structure is affected by the perceived goals of the discourse; analyses and teaching should incorporate pragmatic factors (purpose, audience, institutional constraints).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize historical/procedural origins (inverted pyramid, five W's) but reconsider their fit for comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: The inverted pyramid and Five W's evolved for telegraph-era dispatches and editorial/production constraints; these historical practices shaped news form but are not inevitably optimal for comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand why forms evolved (telegraphing, competition, printing constraints) but evaluate whether they should continue to determine story form if they impede logical organization and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedagogical and production constraints that remove connectives in early texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts used in early reading instruction often mandate very short sentences and no paragraphing; what gets deleted are connective words, producing inexplicit connections among ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate loosening sentence length requirements after basic decoding is achieved to allow more natural use of connectives; hypothesize this may not delay and might hasten acquisition of comprehension skills—experiments are feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach reporters to highlight and enhance natural structure rather than hide flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of teaching reporters cheap tricks to hide a multitude of flaws, instruction should concentrate on highlighting and enhancing whatever natural structure inheres in a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The important question about a story should be 'Is this a logically structured account?' not 'Is it flashy (or zippy or vivid) enough?' Emphasize structure over gimmicks that distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit the point or interpretive connection when it exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there often is a point to a news story, the point is not supposed to be stated explicitly in the news story (journalism students are taught to avoid blurring news and editorial pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a substantive point or explanatory relation exists, writers should not shy away from making the logical connection explicit for readers while maintaining appropriate attribution and professional boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small structural cues (titles, labels) greatly improve comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely adding a title or category label to a text improves comprehensibility (Bransford & Johnson demonstration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minimal but informative structural cues—headers, labels, clear topic markers—to help readers reconstruct intended relations and improve understanding.
